chunks: H-bridge vs half-bridge trade-offs. The question: What is the difference between an H-bridge and half-bridge? What are the tradeoffs?
A half-bridge is one pair of switches with a single output. The load must connect that output to something fixed, such as ground.
An H-bridge is two such pairs, and the load sits between the two outputs.
That extra control of the load's second end is what lets an H-bridge reverse a motor, at the cost of more parts and more loss.
Think of pushing a child on a swing. With a half-bridge you can only push from one side of a fixed post, so the swing goes one way.
With an H-bridge you have a helper on each side, so you can push either way, and you can also hold the swing still. The helper costs a second wage and adds a little drag.
Where it breaks: a half-bridge can still brake a motor by shorting it; it just cannot reverse it.
Only the H-bridge covers the full plus-or-minus range with the full supply.
The split-rail half-bridge covers both polarities but only half the range; the ground-referenced half-bridge is one-sided.
Half-bridge: two switches, one output node. H-bridge (full bridge): two half-bridges with the load floating between their outputs.
Floating load: a load with neither end tied to a fixed rail, so you control both ends.
Conduction loss: heat from current flowing through the small resistance of a switch that is on, P equals I squared R .
Plugging / braking: stopping a motor by shorting it or by driving it backward.
Take a 12 volts supply and a 5 amps load. Each switch that is on has 20 milliohms (0. 02 ohms) of resistance.
A half-bridge with the load to ground has one switch in the current path: 5 squared times 0. 02 equals 0. 5 watts. An H-bridge has two in series: 5 squared times 0. 04 equals 1.
0 watts. The half-bridge gives 0 to 12 volts, so a motor turns one way; the H-bridge gives -12 volts to +12 volts, so it can reverse. That is the whole idea.
"A half-bridge is one leg of two FETs; it drives a load between its output and a fixed rail, so the load sees zero to the supply and a motor only turns one way.

An H-bridge is two legs with the load floating between them, which gives plus or minus the full supply, so reverse, brake and regeneration, but it needs twice the FETs and drivers, and has twice the conduction loss.
Use a half-bridge for fans, solenoids and bucks, an H-bridge for reversing motors and bipolar drive."
